The content does not include discussions of unlabeled uses of products or products under investigational use. 5. Ticks, belonging to the families Ixodidae and Argasidae, are vectors for a variety of pathogens, including bacteria, protozoa, and viruses, which cause numerous diseases in humans and animals. These include rickettsial diseases caused by bacteria in the order Rickettsiales. 6. Vertebrate animals are essential to the life cycle of tick species, while humans serve as incidental hosts. 7. Effective management of tickborne rickettsial diseases requires a comprehensive approach that integrates human, animal, and environmental health, collectively known as the One Health framework. This multidisciplinary approach facilitates understanding of these complex zoonotic diseases. 8. Tickborne rickettsial diseases in humans often present with similar clinical features but are distinct in their epidemiology and causative agents. 9. In the United States, tickborne rickettsial diseases include: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) caused by Rickettsia rickettsii. Other spotted fever group (SFG) rickettsioses caused by Rickettsia parkeri and Rickettsia species 364D. Human monocytic ehrlichiosis caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis. Other ehrlichioses caused by Ehrlichia ewingii and Ehrlichia muris-like (EML) agent. Human granulocytic anaplasmosis caused by Anaplasma phagocytophilum. 10. Rickettsial pathogens transmitted by arthropods other than ticks, such as fleas (Rickettsia typhi), lice (Rickettsia prowazekii), and mites (Rickettsia akari), are not included in this report. 11. Imported tickborne rickettsial infections that may be diagnosed in returning travelers are summarized, but non-tickborne rickettsial illnesses typically encountered outside the United States are not addressed in detail. 12. Despite the availability of low-cost and effective antibacterial therapy, tickborne rickettsial diseases continue to cause severe illness and death in otherwise healthy adults and children. 13. Early recognition of these diseases is critical, as antibacterial therapy is most effective during the initial stages of illness. 14. Early symptoms of tickborne rickettsial diseases are often nonspecific or mimic other illnesses, making diagnosis challenging. 15. Since 2004, three additional agents have been identified as causes of human tickborne rickettsial diseases in the United States: Rickettsia parkeri, Ehrlichia muris-like agent, and Rickettsia species 364D. 16. This report updates the 2006 CDC recommendations on the diagnosis and management of tickborne rickettsial diseases in the United States. It includes practical information on epidemiology, clinical assessment, treatment, laboratory diagnosis, and prevention. 17. The CDC Rickettsial Zoonoses Branch, in collaboration with external clinical and academic specialists and public health professionals, developed this report to assist healthcare providers and public health professionals in: Recognizing key epidemiologic features and clinical manifestations of tickborne rickettsial diseases. Understanding that doxycycline is the treatment of choice for suspected tickborne rickettsial diseases in adults and children. Initiating early empirical antibacterial therapy to prevent severe disease and death. Requesting appropriate confirmatory diagnostic tests and understanding their utility and limitations. Reporting probable and confirmed cases to public health authorities. 18. International travelers are summarized in the report; however, tickborne and non-tickborne rickettsial illnesses typically encountered outside the United States are not addressed in detail. 19. The reported incidence of tickborne rickettsial diseases in the United States has increased over the past decade. 20. Healthcare providers should be familiar with risk factors, signs, and symptoms consistent with tickborne rickettsial diseases to improve early and accurate diagnosis. 21. This report provides practical guidance for healthcare providers and public health professionals to: Recognize the epidemiology and clinical manifestations of tickborne rickettsial diseases. Obtain an appropriate clinical history for suspected cases. Identify severe manifestations of these diseases. Make treatment decisions based on epidemiologic and clinical evidence. Recognize the importance of early and empirical treatment with doxycycline. Understand the availability, limitations, and utility of confirmatory diagnostic tests. Advise patients on tick bite prevention. 22. Additional information on tickborne rickettsial diseases is available from medical and veterinary specialists, various medical and veterinary societies, state and local health authorities, and the CDC. 23. The information and recommendations in this report are intended to provide general guidance for healthcare providers and public health professionals. Individual clinical circumstances should always be considered. 24. This report is not a substitute for professional medical advice for individual patients. Persons with concerns about tickborne rickettsial diseases should seek advice from their healthcare providers. 25. Updated recommendations are needed to address the changing epidemiology of tickborne rickettsial diseases, provide current information about new and emerging pathogens, and highlight advances in diagnostic tests and treatment. 26. The CDC Rickettsial Zoonoses Branch reviewed the 2006 report and identified areas requiring updates or revisions. 27. Internal and external subject-matter experts in tickborne rickettsial diseases, representing a range of professional experiences and viewpoints, contributed to the revision of this report. 28. Peer-reviewed literature, published guidelines, and public health data were reviewed, with particular attention to new material available since the preparation of the previous report. 29. The scientific literature was searched through February 2016 using the MEDLINE database of the National Library of Medicine. 30. Articles selected were in English or had available translations. Peer-reviewed publications and published guidelines were used to support recommendations when possible. 31. When evidence was insufficient for a recommendation, general guidance was provided based on available evidence and expert opinion from the CDC Rickettsial Zoonoses Branch. 32. All contributors had the opportunity to review and provide input on multiple drafts of the report, including the final version. 33. Future updates to this report will be dictated by new data in the field of tickborne rickettsial diseases.
